declared.title: Confidence, Not Consistency, Characterizes Flashbulb Memories
declared.foundIn: reports/memory-rewritten/counter-evidence.md (card 16); OpenAlex search « flashbulb memories everyday memories consistency confidence vividness belief accuracy », to 2004 (2026-11-26)

population: 54 US students who wrote, the next day, how they heard shocking national news (2001) and a recent everyday event; retested 1, 6 or 32 weeks later

findings.text: Both memories changed over time: agreement with one's own first account declined for the emotional memory and for the everyday one, with no difference found between them

support.sentence: Consistency for the flashbulb and everyday memories did not differ, in both cases declining over time.

findings.text: Vividness, recollection and belief in the memory's accuracy declined only for the everyday memory: for the emotional one, belief in its accuracy did not decline while it changed

support.sentence: However, ratings of vividness, recollection, and belief in the accuracy of memory declined only for everyday memories.

findings.text: The authors conclude that emotional « flashbulb » memories are special not in their accuracy (here, agreement with one's first account) but only in how accurate they feel

support.sentence: Flashbulb memories are not special in their accuracy, as previously claimed, but only in their perceived accuracy.

limits: 54 students at one US university: a small sample
the emotional event is a national tragedy: on the evidence page only, never staged in the scene
accuracy is agreement with one's own first account, not checked against what happened
for the everyday memory, belief in its accuracy fell along with its consistency: there, feeling sure did follow the memory
« did not differ » is no difference found, not equality shown: 54 people split across three retest delays, no equivalence test in the abstract
